b:
The first week at college is often a mixture of excitement and anxiety. For many freshmen, it is the first time they have lived away from home, and suddenly they must manage their own schedules, money and meals. Some students adapt quickly, while others feel lonely and confused.
Experts suggest that new students should take the initiative to make friends. Joining a club or a sports team is an effective way to meet people who share similar interests. It is also wise to get familiar with the campus early: find the library, the dining hall and the health center before you actually need them.
Another common challenge is time management. Unlike high school, college courses leave a great deal of free time, and it is easy to waste it. Setting a simple weekly plan can help students balance study, rest and social activities.
Finally, freshmen should remember that feeling uncomfortable at first is perfectly normal. Almost everyone around them is going through the same adjustment. With patience and an open mind, the strange new environment will soon feel like a second home.

tc: 智能手机让我们更孤独了吗？
b:
Smartphones were designed to connect people, yet many researchers now worry that they may be doing the opposite. In restaurants and on buses, it is common to see groups of friends sitting together while each person stares silently at a screen.
A recent survey found that young adults who spend more than five hours a day on their phones are more likely to report feelings of loneliness. However, the relationship is complex. Lonely people may simply use their phones more, rather than phones causing loneliness.
What seems clear is that the quality of online interaction matters. Sending a thoughtful message to a distant friend can strengthen a relationship, while endlessly scrolling through other people's photos often leads to comparison and dissatisfaction.
Some people have started to establish "phone-free" times, such as during meals or the hour before bed. They report sleeping better and paying more attention to the people around them. The lesson is not that technology is evil, but that we should use it consciously instead of letting it control our time and emotions.

tc: 为什么城市需要更多树木
b:
Trees are often regarded as decoration in modern cities, but scientists argue that they provide essential services. First, trees reduce temperatures. On hot summer days, streets lined with trees can be several degrees cooler than those without shade, which lowers the demand for air conditioning.
Second, trees improve air quality by absorbing pollutants and producing oxygen. They also capture rainwater with their roots, reducing the risk of floods after heavy storms.
The benefits are not only physical. Studies show that people who live near green spaces tend to experience less stress and recover faster from illness. Even a view of trees from a hospital window has been linked to shorter hospital stays.
Despite these advantages, urban trees face many threats, including construction, disease and limited space for roots to grow. Some cities have responded by launching tree-planting campaigns and encouraging residents to adopt and care for trees on their streets.
Planting a tree is a small action, but when millions of people participate, the result can transform a city into a healthier and more pleasant place to live.

t: The Hidden Cost of Staying Up Late
b:
Many university students are proud of staying up late. They study, chat or play games until two or three in the morning and believe they can make up for lost sleep at the weekend. Unfortunately, the human body does not work that way.
Sleep is when the brain organizes and stores the information we have learned during the day. Without enough sleep, our memory and concentration suffer. Students who sleep less than six hours a night often perform worse on exams, even if they spend more time studying.
Lack of sleep also affects mood and health. It increases the risk of anxiety, weakens the immune system and can lead to weight gain, because tired people tend to crave sugary foods.
Doctors recommend that young adults sleep seven to nine hours a night and keep a regular schedule. Simple habits can help: avoid caffeine in the evening, put the phone away before bed, and keep the bedroom dark and quiet.
Getting enough sleep is not a sign of laziness. On the contrary, it is one of the most effective ways to improve both academic performance and overall well-being.

In an age of fast food and online shopping, traditional festivals still hold a special place in people's hearts. During the Spring Festival, millions of Chinese people travel long distances to reunite with their families, creating the largest annual migration on earth.
Festivals are more than holidays. They carry history, values and shared memories. The Mid-Autumn Festival, for example, expresses the wish for family harmony through mooncakes and the full moon, while the Dragon Boat Festival honours a poet who loved his country.
However, some people worry that festivals are becoming too commercial. Advertising encourages expensive gifts, and the original meaning is sometimes forgotten. Young people may know more about Western holidays than about their own customs.
To keep traditions alive, schools and communities have organized activities such as making dumplings, writing couplets and learning folk songs. Social media has also helped, as young people share creative ways of celebrating.
Traditions survive not by staying unchanged but by adapting to new times while preserving their core spirit. When we celebrate thoughtfully, festivals continue to connect generations and give us a sense of belonging.

Many graduates believe that good grades are the key to a good job. While academic achievement certainly matters, surveys of employers suggest that they value other qualities just as highly.
Communication skills consistently rank near the top. Employers want people who can express ideas clearly, listen carefully and write professional emails. Teamwork is another essential ability, since most modern jobs require cooperation across departments.
Employers also look for problem-solving skills and a willingness to learn. Technology changes so rapidly that specific knowledge can become outdated within a few years. A candidate who can adapt and acquire new skills is therefore more valuable than one who simply memorizes facts.
Finally, attitude counts. Responsibility, honesty and a positive approach to challenges make a strong impression during interviews and internships.
For students, the message is clear: while studying hard, they should also take part in group projects, volunteer work and part-time jobs. These experiences provide opportunities to develop the practical skills that will help them stand out in a competitive job market.

Why can we remember a song from childhood but forget a word we learned yesterday? The answer lies in how the brain processes memory.
When we encounter new information, it first enters short-term memory, which can hold only a few items for a short time. To move information into long-term memory, the brain needs repetition and meaning. The more connections a new fact has with what we already know, the easier it is to recall.
In the nineteenth century, the psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus discovered the "forgetting curve". He found that we forget most new information within a day unless we review it. However, each review slows down the rate of forgetting.
This discovery led to a powerful learning method called spaced repetition. Instead of studying a word ten times in one evening, learners review it after one day, then three days, then a week, and so on. This approach saves time and produces lasting results.
Emotion also plays a role. Experiences that make us happy, surprised or frightened are remembered more vividly. So, if you want to remember something, try to make it personal, interesting and meaningful.

Thanks to better medicine and living conditions, people today live much longer than before. While this is a great achievement, it also creates new challenges for society.
As the number of elderly people grows and birth rates fall, there are fewer young workers to support each retired person. This puts pressure on pension systems and health care services. Many families also struggle to look after aging parents while raising their own children and working full-time.
Governments are exploring various solutions. Some have raised the retirement age, while others encourage community care centres where seniors can receive meals, medical checks and companionship during the day.
Technology may help as well. Smart devices can remind older people to take medicine, detect falls and allow them to video-chat with relatives who live far away.
Yet the most important factor may be our attitude. Older people are not merely a burden; they possess valuable experience and wisdom. Many are eager to volunteer, teach or continue working. A society that respects and involves its seniors will be better prepared for the future.

t: The Value of Reading Paper Books
b:
With e-books and audiobooks available on every phone, some people predict that paper books will soon disappear. However, sales of printed books have remained surprisingly stable, and many readers still prefer the feel of real pages.
Research offers some support for this preference. Several studies have found that people understand and remember long texts better when reading on paper. One explanation is that a physical book provides a sense of location: readers can recall that an idea appeared near the top of a left-hand page, which helps them build a mental map of the content.
Screens, on the other hand, encourage skimming. Notifications and links constantly distract us, making deep reading more difficult.
That does not mean digital reading is useless. E-books are convenient, cheap and easy to carry, and they allow readers to adjust font size or look up words instantly.
Perhaps the best approach is to choose the format according to the purpose. For quick information, a screen works well. For serious study or a novel you want to enjoy slowly, a paper book may still be the better companion.

Plastic is cheap, light and durable, which is exactly why it has become a serious environmental problem. Every year, millions of tons of plastic waste end up in rivers and oceans, where it can remain for hundreds of years.
Sea animals often mistake plastic bags for food. Turtles, birds and whales have been found with stomachs full of plastic, which can cause them to starve. Over time, large pieces break down into tiny particles called microplastics, which have been detected in drinking water, salt and even human blood.
Many countries have taken action. Some charge a fee for plastic bags, while others have banned single-use plastic straws and cups. Companies are also developing packaging made from plants that can decompose naturally.
Individuals can contribute too. Carrying a reusable bottle and shopping bag, refusing unnecessary packaging and sorting rubbish correctly are simple habits that make a difference when practised by many people.
Plastic itself is not the enemy; it is our throwaway culture that needs to change. By reducing, reusing and recycling, we can enjoy the benefits of plastic without destroying the planet.

tc: 机器人会抢走我们的工作吗？
b:
Artificial intelligence and robots are developing at an astonishing speed. They can now drive cars, translate languages and even write articles. Naturally, many workers are anxious about whether their jobs will survive.
History offers some comfort. When machines replaced farm workers in the past, new industries emerged and created millions of new positions. Technology tends to eliminate certain tasks rather than entire professions.
Jobs that involve repetitive, predictable work are the most likely to be automated. In contrast, occupations requiring creativity, emotional understanding and complex judgment, such as nursing, teaching and design, are much harder for machines to perform.
Nevertheless, the transition may be painful for some people. Workers who lose their jobs may need retraining, and governments will have to provide support during the change.
For students, the best strategy is to develop abilities that complement technology instead of competing with it. Learning to work with AI tools, thinking critically and communicating well will be essential skills in the future workplace.

tc: 早餐真的是最重要的一餐吗？
b:
We have all heard that breakfast is the most important meal of the day. Yet in busy modern life, many young people skip it, rushing to class or work with an empty stomach.
Supporters of breakfast argue that it provides the energy needed to start the day. After a night without food, the body's blood sugar is low, and eating in the morning helps the brain concentrate. Some studies have shown that students who eat breakfast perform better in morning tests.
However, recent research suggests the picture is more complicated. For healthy adults, what you eat may matter more than when you eat. A breakfast of sweet pastries and sugary drinks may cause energy to crash an hour later.
Nutritionists recommend a balanced breakfast that combines protein, whole grains and fruit, such as eggs, oatmeal and a banana. Even something simple like milk and whole-wheat bread is better than nothing.
In the end, the key is to listen to your body and develop regular eating habits. A healthy breakfast is a small investment that can bring a better mood and higher efficiency throughout the day.

Some of the most valuable lessons are not learned in a classroom but on the road. Travel exposes us to different cultures, foods and ways of thinking, broadening our view of the world.
When we visit a new place, we are forced to solve problems on our own: finding our way in an unfamiliar city, communicating in a foreign language and adjusting our plans when things go wrong. These experiences build independence and confidence.
Travel also teaches tolerance. Meeting people whose customs differ from ours helps us realize that there is more than one "right" way to live. Many travellers return home with a deeper appreciation of both other cultures and their own.
Of course, travel does not have to be expensive. Students can explore nearby towns, join exchange programmes or volunteer abroad. What matters is not the distance but the attitude: curiosity, respect and a willingness to step outside one's comfort zone.
As an old saying goes, "Travelling ten thousand miles is better than reading ten thousand books." Ideally, we should do both.

Many young people find it difficult to manage their money. With online shopping available around the clock and payment as easy as scanning a code, it is tempting to spend without thinking.
A growing number of students now rely on credit products to buy phones, clothes and concert tickets. While borrowing can be useful in emergencies, unplanned debt can quickly become a heavy burden and cause considerable stress.
Financial experts suggest starting with a simple budget. Write down your monthly income, then list necessary expenses such as food and transport. Whatever remains can be divided between savings and entertainment.
Another useful habit is waiting before buying. If you still want an item after 24 hours, it may be worth purchasing; if not, you have saved money and avoided an impulse purchase.
Learning about money early has long-term benefits. Even small savings grow over time, and good habits formed at university will provide security and freedom in the future. Money management is not about being stingy; it is about making choices that reflect what you truly value.

t: The Benefits of Exercise for Students
b:
When exams approach, many students cut back on exercise to make more time for studying. Ironically, this may harm their academic performance.
Physical activity increases blood flow to the brain, supplying it with oxygen and nutrients. Research shows that even a 20-minute walk can improve attention and memory for several hours afterwards. Regular exercise also stimulates the growth of new brain cells in areas related to learning.
Exercise is also a powerful tool for managing stress. It releases chemicals that improve mood and helps people sleep more deeply. Students who exercise regularly report feeling less anxious and more confident.
The good news is that exercise does not have to be intense. Jogging, cycling, dancing or playing basketball with friends all count. The key is consistency: about 30 minutes a day, five days a week, is enough to produce noticeable benefits.
So the next time you feel tired after hours of reviewing, put down your books and go for a run. You may find that you return to your desk with a clearer mind and renewed energy.

Volunteering means offering time and skills to help others without expecting payment. Every year, millions of young people volunteer in communities, schools, hospitals and disaster areas.
The benefits for those who receive help are obvious, but volunteers gain a great deal as well. Helping others gives people a sense of purpose and satisfaction. Studies have even found that regular volunteers tend to be happier and healthier.
Volunteering is also an excellent way to develop practical skills. Organizing an event, teaching children or working with people from different backgrounds improves communication, leadership and problem-solving abilities. Many employers view volunteer experience positively.
Furthermore, volunteering helps young people understand social issues more deeply. When students teach in rural schools or visit elderly people living alone, they gain a real understanding of challenges that they might otherwise only read about.
Of course, good volunteering requires responsibility. Volunteers should be reliable, respect the people they serve and make a long-term commitment when possible. Small acts of kindness, repeated over time, can make a lasting difference.

Bees are small, but their role in nature is enormous. As they fly from flower to flower collecting nectar, they carry pollen, allowing plants to produce fruit and seeds. Roughly one third of the food we eat depends on this process, known as pollination.
Unfortunately, bee populations have declined sharply in many parts of the world. Scientists have identified several causes, including the loss of wild flowers, the use of pesticides, disease and climate change.
If bees continue to disappear, the consequences could be serious. Prices of fruits and vegetables such as apples, strawberries and almonds might rise, and the variety of food available could shrink.
Fortunately, there are ways to help. Farmers can reduce pesticide use and plant strips of flowers around their fields. Cities can create bee-friendly parks, and individuals can grow flowers on balconies.
Protecting bees is not only about saving one species. It reminds us that everything in nature is connected, and that human survival depends on the health of the ecosystems around us.

Tea is one of the most popular drinks in the world, second only to water. Its history begins in China, where, according to legend, leaves accidentally fell into boiling water more than four thousand years ago.
Over the centuries, tea became deeply rooted in Chinese culture. Poets wrote about it, scholars discussed it, and special ceremonies developed around its preparation. The famous Tea Horse Road once carried tea across mountains to distant regions in exchange for horses.
Tea later spread along trade routes to Japan, the Middle East and Europe. In Britain, it became a national habit, giving rise to the tradition of afternoon tea. Each culture adapted tea to its own tastes, adding milk, sugar, spices or mint.
Today, scientists have found that tea contains substances that may benefit health, such as antioxidants that protect cells.
More than a drink, tea is a symbol of hospitality and calm. Offering a cup of tea to a guest expresses respect, and sharing tea with friends creates a moment of peace in a busy day.

Online shopping has changed the way we live. With a few taps on a phone, we can buy almost anything and have it delivered to our door, sometimes within hours.
Convenience is the main attraction. Consumers can compare prices easily, read reviews from other buyers and shop at any time of the day. For people living in remote areas, online platforms provide access to products that were once unavailable.
However, online shopping has its drawbacks. Because buying is so easy, many people make impulse purchases and end up with items they do not need. The large amount of packaging also creates environmental problems, and the rapid growth of delivery services has placed heavy pressure on workers.
Physical stores have suffered as well. Many small shops have closed, changing the character of city streets. In response, some retailers now combine online and offline services, letting customers order online and pick up in store.
Online shopping is here to stay. The challenge is to enjoy its convenience while shopping responsibly and supporting a fair and sustainable system.

t: Overcoming the Fear of Public Speaking
b:
For many people, speaking in front of an audience is more frightening than almost anything else. Their hearts beat faster, their hands shake and their minds go blank.
This fear is natural. Our ancestors depended on acceptance by the group, so the possibility of being judged by many people triggers an ancient alarm in the brain. The good news is that this fear can be managed.
Preparation is the most effective weapon. Speakers who know their material well feel more confident. Practising aloud several times, preferably in front of a friend, helps identify weak points.
It also helps to change how we view nervousness. Instead of thinking "I am scared", try telling yourself "I am excited". Research suggests this simple shift can improve performance.
During the speech, focus on the message rather than on yourself. Make eye contact with friendly faces, speak slowly and pause to breathe.
Finally, remember that the audience generally wants you to succeed. Every confident speaker you admire was once a nervous beginner. With practice, public speaking can become not only bearable but enjoyable.

Climate change may sound like a distant problem discussed by scientists and politicians, but its effects are increasingly visible in daily life. Summers are getting hotter, heavy rains are more frequent, and some regions suffer from long droughts.
The main cause is the burning of fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas, which releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. This gas traps heat and gradually raises the earth's temperature.
Rising temperatures affect agriculture, water supplies and human health. Farmers face unpredictable harvests, and heatwaves are dangerous for the elderly and children.
Solving the problem requires large-scale action, such as developing renewable energy and improving public transport. But individuals also have a role. Choosing to walk or cycle for short trips, saving electricity, eating less meat and avoiding waste all reduce our carbon footprint.
It is easy to feel that one person cannot make a difference. Yet social change often starts with individual choices that gradually become new norms. When millions of people change their habits, governments and companies pay attention.

Stress is a normal part of life. A certain amount of pressure can even be helpful, pushing us to prepare for an exam or finish a project on time. However, when stress becomes constant, it can damage both physical and mental health.
Common signs of excessive stress include trouble sleeping, headaches, loss of appetite and difficulty concentrating. Some people become easily irritated or withdraw from friends.
Psychologists recommend several strategies. First, identify the source of stress and break big problems into smaller, manageable steps. Second, take care of the body: regular exercise, enough sleep and healthy food make us more resilient.
Third, talk to someone. Sharing worries with a friend, family member or counsellor can relieve pressure and offer new perspectives. Many universities provide free psychological services for students.
Finally, make time for activities you enjoy, whether it is music, drawing or walking in nature. These moments of relaxation are not a waste of time; they recharge our energy. Learning to manage stress is a skill that will benefit us throughout our lives.

Online courses have become a common part of education. Students can watch lectures at any time, replay difficult sections and learn from top teachers around the world.
The flexibility of online learning is its greatest strength. Working adults can study in the evening, and students in remote areas can access high-quality resources that were once available only in big cities.
However, online learning also presents challenges. Without a teacher watching, students must rely on self-discipline, and many find it easy to fall behind. Completion rates for free online courses are often very low.
The lack of face-to-face interaction is another drawback. Discussions with classmates and immediate feedback from teachers are important for deeper understanding and motivation.
Many educators believe the future lies in "blended learning", which combines online materials with classroom activities. Students watch lectures at home and use class time for discussion, projects and practice.
For learners, success online depends on good habits: setting clear goals, following a fixed schedule and actively participating in forums. Used wisely, online learning can be a powerful tool.

In recent years, the sharing economy has spread rapidly. People now share bicycles, cars, rooms and even power banks through mobile apps, paying only for the time they use them.
The idea is attractive. Sharing makes better use of resources that would otherwise sit idle, reduces costs for consumers and creates income for owners. Shared bicycles, for instance, have made short trips in cities easier and greener.
However, the rapid expansion has also caused problems. In some cities, thousands of broken bikes piled up on pavements, blocking roads and wasting resources. Questions about safety, insurance and the protection of workers' rights have also emerged.
Governments have responded by introducing regulations, such as limiting the number of bikes and requiring companies to manage parking.
The sharing economy reflects a change in attitudes: many young people now value access over ownership. To develop healthily, however, it needs responsible companies, sensible rules and users who respect shared property.

Space exploration is extremely expensive, and some people question whether the money would be better spent solving problems on earth. Supporters, however, argue that exploring space brings many benefits.
First, space research has produced technologies that we use every day, from weather forecasting and satellite navigation to improved medical equipment and water purification systems.
Second, studying other planets helps us understand our own. By observing how the climate of Mars changed, for example, scientists gain insights into processes that could affect the earth.
Third, space exploration inspires people. When astronauts walk in space or a rover lands on a distant planet, millions of young people become interested in science and engineering.
Finally, some scientists believe that, in the long term, humans may need to live on other planets to ensure the survival of our species.
Space exploration is a reflection of human curiosity, the same desire that drove our ancestors to cross oceans. Exploring the unknown is part of what makes us human.

Watching films in English is one of the most enjoyable ways to improve language skills. Films expose learners to natural speech, including everyday expressions, humour and different accents that textbooks rarely include.
To make the most of film watching, choose movies that match your level. Animated films and family comedies usually use clear, simple language, making them a good starting point.
Subtitles can help, but they should be used wisely. At first, English subtitles allow you to connect sounds with written words. As your listening improves, try turning them off for short scenes.
Active watching is more effective than passive viewing. Pause the film to repeat interesting lines, imitate the actors' pronunciation and note useful phrases. Watching the same scene several times can greatly improve listening comprehension.
Films also offer cultural insight, showing how people live, joke and express emotions in English-speaking countries.
Of course, films alone are not enough to master a language. But combined with reading, vocabulary study and speaking practice, they can make learning English a real pleasure.

For most college students, sharing a dormitory room is a new experience. Living with someone from a different background can be rewarding, but it can also lead to conflicts over noise, cleanliness and personal space.
Many problems arise simply because roommates have different habits. One person may like to go to bed early, while the other studies late into the night. One may be very tidy, while the other leaves clothes everywhere.
The key to a peaceful relationship is communication. At the beginning of the term, roommates should discuss their expectations openly: when to keep quiet, how to share cleaning duties and whether guests are welcome.
When problems occur, it is better to address them calmly and early rather than letting resentment build up. Using "I" statements, such as "I find it hard to sleep when the light is on," sounds less like an accusation.
Respect and flexibility are also important. Nobody is perfect, and small compromises make daily life much easier. In fact, many people find that their college roommates become lifelong friends.

Every time we search the Internet, use an app or post on social media, we leave a trail of personal information. Companies collect this data to target advertisements, and in some cases it may be stolen by criminals.
Many users are unaware of how much information they reveal. A photo can show where you live, and a quiz on social media might collect details that help someone guess your password.
There are several simple steps to protect privacy. First, use strong and different passwords for important accounts, and turn on two-step verification. Second, check the privacy settings of apps and limit their access to your location, contacts and camera.
Third, think before you share. Avoid posting your phone number, address or travel plans publicly. Be careful with links in unexpected messages, as they may lead to fake websites designed to steal information.
Governments are also passing laws that require companies to protect user data and explain how it is used. Still, personal awareness remains the first line of defence. In the digital age, protecting privacy is a basic life skill.

Water makes up about sixty percent of the human body, and it plays a part in almost every function, from regulating temperature to carrying nutrients and removing waste. Yet many people do not drink enough.
Even mild dehydration can cause tiredness, headaches and difficulty concentrating. Students who feel sleepy in afternoon classes may simply need a glass of water rather than another cup of coffee.
How much water do we need? A common recommendation is about eight glasses a day, but the right amount depends on body size, activity and climate. People who exercise or live in hot places need more.
Sugary drinks are not a good substitute. Soft drinks and sweet teas contain large amounts of sugar, which increases the risk of obesity and tooth decay.
To build a healthy habit, carry a reusable water bottle and drink regularly throughout the day instead of waiting until you feel thirsty. Fruit and vegetables such as watermelon and cucumber also provide water.
It is one of the simplest and cheapest ways to protect your health.

Every year, large numbers of young people move to big cities in search of better jobs and opportunities. Cities offer higher salaries, excellent universities, cultural events and an exciting lifestyle.
However, city life also has its price. Housing is expensive, and many young workers share small apartments or spend hours commuting. Traffic jams, crowded subways and air pollution can make daily life exhausting.
Competition is intense, and the fast pace can create a sense of pressure. Some people feel lonely despite being surrounded by millions of others.
In recent years, some young people have chosen to leave big cities for smaller towns, where the cost of living is lower and life is more relaxed. Remote work has made this choice easier for some professions.
There is no single right answer. Big cities suit those who seek challenge and diversity, while smaller places appeal to those who value space and balance. The important thing is to understand one's own priorities before deciding where to build a life.

For a long time, people believed that intelligence was a uniquely human quality. However, scientific research has revealed that many animals are far smarter than we once thought.
Chimpanzees use sticks as tools to catch insects, and crows can bend wires into hooks to reach food. Dolphins call each other by individual whistles, similar to names. Elephants appear to mourn their dead, returning to the bones of family members.
Even smaller creatures show surprising abilities. Bees communicate the location of flowers through a special dance, and octopuses can open jars and escape from tanks.
These discoveries have changed how we think about animals. If animals can feel, remember and solve problems, then we have a greater responsibility to treat them well.
They also teach us that intelligence takes many forms. Instead of asking whether animals are as clever as humans, scientists now ask how each species has developed abilities suited to its environment. The natural world, it seems, is full of minds waiting to be understood.

Internships give students a chance to experience real work before they graduate. For many, it is the first time they apply classroom knowledge to practical problems.
An internship helps students understand what a job really involves. Some discover a passion for a field, while others realize that a career they had imagined is not suitable for them. Both outcomes are valuable, as they help guide future choices.
Internships also build skills and connections. Interns learn how to communicate with colleagues, meet deadlines and behave professionally. Supervisors may later provide recommendation letters, and some companies offer full-time positions to excellent interns.
To make the most of an internship, students should be proactive. Ask questions, volunteer for tasks and seek feedback. Keeping a record of projects and achievements makes it easier to write a strong résumé later.
However, students should also be aware of their rights. An internship should be a learning experience, not simply a source of cheap labour. Choosing reputable organizations and clarifying responsibilities in advance can prevent disappointment.

Food is much more than fuel for the body. It reflects geography, history and the values of a community. When people move to a new country, the dishes they cook often become a powerful link to home.
Different regions develop unique cuisines based on local ingredients and climate. In China, for example, northern areas are famous for noodles and dumplings made from wheat, while southern regions rely more on rice.
Meals also carry social meaning. Sharing food is a way of showing friendship and respect, and many celebrations centre on special dishes. Families pass recipes from generation to generation, preserving memories along with flavours.
Globalization has made it possible to taste foods from around the world without travelling. This exchange enriches our lives, though some worry that traditional dishes may be replaced by standardized fast food.
Learning to cook a traditional dish is a meaningful way to connect with one's roots. And trying the food of another culture with an open mind is often the first step toward understanding its people.

Transport is one of the largest sources of greenhouse gas emissions, mainly because of the huge number of private cars on the road. Choosing greener ways to travel can make a significant difference.
For short distances, walking and cycling are the best choices. They produce no pollution, cost little and improve fitness. Many cities have built bike lanes and pedestrian streets to encourage these options.
Public transport is another effective solution. A single bus or subway train can carry dozens or hundreds of passengers, using far less energy per person than private cars.
Electric vehicles are becoming increasingly popular as battery technology improves and charging stations become more common. Their environmental benefits are greatest when the electricity comes from clean sources such as wind and solar power.
Changing travel habits is not always easy, especially in places with poor public transport. But governments can help by investing in infrastructure, and individuals can start with small steps, such as cycling to class once a week. Every green trip counts.

Taking notes is one of the most important skills for success at university, yet few students are ever taught how to do it well.
Many students try to write down everything the lecturer says. This is not only impossible but also ineffective, because it leaves no time to think. Good notes capture the main ideas, key terms and examples in a brief form.
One popular approach is the Cornell method. The page is divided into three parts: a wide column for notes during the lecture, a narrow column for questions and keywords added later, and a section at the bottom for a short summary. This structure encourages active review.
Research suggests that writing by hand may help memory more than typing, because writing slowly forces us to process and summarize information instead of copying it word for word.
The most important step happens after class. Reviewing notes within twenty-four hours, filling in gaps and testing yourself on key points greatly increases how much you remember. Notes are not just a record; they are a tool for learning.

Not long ago, travellers relied on paper maps and asked strangers for directions. Today, satellite navigation tells us exactly where we are and how to reach our destination.
Navigation systems work by receiving signals from several satellites orbiting the earth. By measuring how long each signal takes to arrive, a receiver can calculate its position with remarkable accuracy.
Beyond helping drivers, satellite navigation has countless applications. Delivery companies use it to plan routes, farmers use it to guide machines across fields, and rescue teams use it to locate people in danger. It also provides precise timing for banking systems and mobile networks.
China's BeiDou system now offers global coverage, giving users another reliable source of positioning services.
However, depending too much on navigation may weaken our natural sense of direction. Some studies suggest that people who always follow digital instructions remember less about their surroundings. Occasionally exploring a place without a phone can be both a good exercise for the brain and an adventure.

When people feel unwell, many choose to treat themselves rather than visit a doctor. They take medicine left over from a previous illness or follow advice found online.
While this may seem convenient, self-medication can be risky. Symptoms such as headache or fever can result from many different causes, and taking the wrong medicine may hide a serious condition.
A particular concern is the misuse of antibiotics. Antibiotics are effective against bacteria, but they do nothing against viruses such as the common cold. Using them unnecessarily helps bacteria become resistant, making future infections harder to treat.
Medicines can also interact with each other. Taking two products that contain the same ingredient can lead to an accidental overdose.
This does not mean we must see a doctor for every minor problem. For simple conditions, a pharmacist can offer reliable advice. The important thing is to read labels carefully, follow the recommended dosage and seek professional help when symptoms are severe or last longer than expected.

t: Reading Habits in the Digital Age
b:
Surveys show that people today read more words than ever before, mainly on screens. However, much of this reading consists of short messages, news headlines and social media posts.
Some experts worry that constant exposure to short content is changing the way our brains process information. People may find it harder to concentrate on long, complex texts and prefer quick summaries instead.
Deep reading, which involves following a long argument or getting lost in a novel, develops important abilities such as critical thinking, imagination and empathy. If we lose this skill, we may become more easily influenced by superficial information.
Fortunately, reading habits can be trained. Setting aside a regular time to read without distractions, starting with books that genuinely interest you and joining a reading group can all help.
Libraries and bookstores are also adapting, offering comfortable spaces and events to attract readers.
In a world full of information, the ability to read deeply is more valuable than ever. It allows us not only to collect facts but to understand them.

Everyone has the same twenty-four hours a day, yet some people accomplish far more than others. The difference often lies in how they manage their time.
A useful starting point is to distinguish between urgent and important tasks. Many people spend their days reacting to urgent matters, such as messages and minor requests, while neglecting important goals that have no immediate deadline. Successful people deliberately schedule time for what matters most.
Another effective technique is breaking large tasks into smaller steps. A thesis that seems overwhelming becomes manageable when divided into reading, outlining and writing one section at a time.
Procrastination is the greatest enemy of good time management. One popular method to overcome it is the Pomodoro Technique: work with full concentration for twenty-five minutes, then take a five-minute break.
Finally, remember that rest is part of a good schedule. Working without breaks leads to exhaustion and lower efficiency. Time management is not about filling every minute, but about using time wisely to achieve a balanced and meaningful life.

Thousands of species around the world are in danger of extinction. The main causes are human activities, including destroying habitats, hunting, pollution and climate change.
Every species plays a role in its ecosystem. When one disappears, others that depend on it may also be affected, creating a chain reaction that weakens the entire system.
Conservation efforts have achieved some notable successes. The giant panda, once considered endangered, has seen its population increase thanks to the protection of bamboo forests and breeding programmes. Its status was officially improved to "vulnerable".
Protecting wildlife requires cooperation at many levels. Governments establish nature reserves and enforce laws against illegal trade. Scientists study animal populations and their needs. Local communities can benefit from eco-tourism, giving them a reason to protect the environment.
Individuals can help too, by refusing to buy products made from endangered animals and supporting conservation organizations.
Preserving biodiversity is not only a moral duty but also essential for our own survival, since healthy ecosystems provide clean water, fertile soil and medicine.

In schools, art and music classes are often the first to be cut when time and money are limited. Yet art plays an important role in personal development and society.
Creating art encourages imagination and original thinking. When students paint a picture or compose a song, there is no single correct answer, so they learn to explore, experiment and accept mistakes as part of the process.
Art is also a powerful means of expression. It allows people to communicate feelings that are difficult to put into words. Many people find that drawing or playing an instrument helps them relax and cope with stress.
On a broader level, art preserves culture and history. Paintings, poems and music from the past tell us how people lived and what they valued. Art can also challenge society by raising questions about injustice.
Furthermore, creative industries such as design, film and gaming provide millions of jobs.
Rather than being a luxury, art is a fundamental part of being human. Everyone, not only professional artists, can benefit from making it part of their lives.

Many Chinese students can read and write English well but feel nervous when they have to speak. They worry about making mistakes, having a strange accent or being laughed at by classmates.
It is important to understand that mistakes are a natural part of learning. Even native speakers make errors in conversation. Teachers are usually far more interested in whether students can communicate ideas than in perfect grammar.
Practice in a low-pressure setting can build confidence. Students can start by reading aloud alone, recording their voices or talking with a partner before speaking in front of the whole class.
Preparing a few useful phrases also helps. Expressions such as "In my opinion", "Could you say that again?" and "Let me think for a moment" give speakers time to organize their thoughts.
Joining an English corner or language exchange provides more opportunities to speak in a relaxed environment.
Each small success makes the next attempt easier. Over time, shy learners often discover that speaking English is not frightening at all, but a pleasant way to share ideas and make friends.

For more than a century, the world has relied mainly on coal, oil and natural gas for energy. These fossil fuels have powered economic growth, but they also cause air pollution and climate change.
Clean energy sources, such as solar, wind and hydropower, offer an alternative. In recent years, the cost of solar panels and wind turbines has fallen dramatically, making them competitive with traditional power plants in many places.
However, renewable energy faces a key challenge: the sun does not always shine, and the wind does not always blow. Storing energy is therefore essential. Engineers are developing better batteries and other storage technologies to supply electricity when production is low.
Upgrading electricity grids is also necessary to transport power from sunny or windy regions to cities far away.
The transition to clean energy will require large investments, but it also creates new industries and jobs. Many countries have set goals to reduce carbon emissions significantly in the coming decades. The future of energy, it seems, will be cleaner, smarter and more diverse.

The structure of families has changed considerably over the past few decades. In the past, several generations often lived under one roof. Today, small nuclear families consisting of parents and one or two children are common.
Several factors have contributed to this change. People move to cities for work, housing is limited, and many young adults value independence. Couples are also marrying later and having fewer children.
These changes bring both benefits and challenges. Smaller families may enjoy more privacy and freedom, and parents can devote more resources to each child. On the other hand, elderly parents may feel lonely when their children live far away, and young parents may lack help with childcare.
Technology has helped families stay connected. Video calls allow grandparents to watch grandchildren grow, even across great distances.
Despite these changes, the core values of family remain the same: love, support and responsibility. Whatever form a family takes, it continues to be a source of strength and belonging for most people.

Mental health is just as important as physical health, yet it is often ignored or misunderstood. Many people hesitate to seek help for anxiety or depression because they fear being judged.
Mental health problems are common among young people. The pressure of exams, uncertainty about the future and difficulties in relationships can all take a toll. Recognizing the signs early is important: persistent sadness, loss of interest in activities, changes in sleep and difficulty concentrating may indicate a problem.
Talking about feelings is not a sign of weakness. On the contrary, reaching out to friends, family or professional counsellors shows courage and self-awareness. Most universities offer counselling services, and many problems can be effectively treated.
Daily habits also support mental well-being. Regular exercise, enough sleep, time in nature and meaningful social connections all help.
We can also support others by listening without judgment and encouraging them to seek help when needed. Creating an environment where people feel safe discussing mental health benefits everyone.

Many young people dream of starting their own businesses. Being your own boss promises freedom, creativity and the chance to turn an idea into reality.
However, entrepreneurship is far from easy. A large proportion of new businesses fail within their first few years. Common reasons include lack of market research, poor financial planning and underestimating competition.
Successful entrepreneurs usually begin by identifying a real problem that people are willing to pay to solve. They test their ideas on a small scale before investing large sums of money, and they listen carefully to customer feedback.
Personal qualities matter as well. Starting a business requires persistence, the ability to handle uncertainty and a willingness to learn from failure. Many famous entrepreneurs experienced several failures before achieving success.
Governments and universities increasingly support young entrepreneurs through training programmes, low-interest loans and business incubators.
Even if a business does not succeed, the experience can be highly valuable. The skills gained, such as leadership, problem-solving and resilience, are useful in any career.

The ocean covers more than seventy percent of the earth's surface, yet more than eighty percent of it remains unexplored. In some ways, we know more about the surface of the moon than about the deep sea.
Exploring the deep ocean is extremely difficult. The pressure at the bottom is enormous, the water is freezing cold and there is no sunlight. Special submarines and robots are needed to reach these depths.
Despite these challenges, scientists continue to make astonishing discoveries. Strange creatures that produce their own light live in the darkness, and entire ecosystems survive around hot springs on the sea floor without any energy from the sun.
The ocean also plays a key role in regulating the earth's climate. It absorbs large amounts of heat and carbon dioxide and produces much of the oxygen we breathe.
Unfortunately, overfishing, pollution and rising temperatures threaten ocean life. Protecting the sea is essential not only for marine creatures but for the future of humanity. There is still so much to learn from this vast blue world.

t: Learning a Foreign Language Opens Doors
tc: 学外语打开新世界的大门
b:
Learning a foreign language is often seen as a practical skill for getting a better job or passing an exam. While these benefits are real, language learning offers much more.
Knowing another language allows us to communicate directly with people from different cultures, making travel richer and friendships possible across borders. It also gives access to books, films and information that are not available in translation.
Research suggests that learning languages benefits the brain. Bilingual people often perform better at tasks requiring attention and switching between activities, and language learning may even delay memory decline in old age.
Perhaps most importantly, a new language offers a new way of seeing the world. Each language organizes ideas differently, and learning one helps us notice assumptions in our own way of thinking.
Of course, language learning takes time and effort. Progress may seem slow at first, but regular practice gradually brings results. As the saying goes, a different language is a different vision of life.

Many cities now require residents to sort their household waste into different categories, such as recyclables, kitchen waste, hazardous waste and other waste.
At first, some people found the rules confusing and inconvenient. Is a used napkin recyclable? Where should old batteries go? Over time, however, many residents have become familiar with the system, and sorting has become a daily habit.
Sorting rubbish has clear benefits. Recyclable materials such as paper, glass and metal can be processed and reused, saving natural resources and energy. Kitchen waste can be turned into fertilizer or biogas. Separating hazardous items like batteries prevents toxic substances from polluting soil and water.
For the system to work, every link in the chain must function properly. Residents need to sort correctly, and collection and processing facilities must keep the categories separate.
Ultimately, the best way to deal with waste is to produce less of it. By buying only what we need and reusing items whenever possible, we can reduce the burden on the environment.

t: Should Students Choose Majors by Interest?
b:
Choosing a major is one of the most important decisions students make. Some advise following personal interests, while others recommend focusing on fields with good employment prospects.
Those who emphasize interest argue that students who enjoy their subjects study harder and perform better. Passion also helps people persist through difficulties, which leads to long-term success.
Others take a more practical view. They point out that some popular interests may offer limited job opportunities, and graduates need to support themselves.
In reality, the two approaches need not conflict. Interests can develop through exposure, and many people come to love a field after studying it seriously. Moreover, many skills learned in university, such as critical thinking and writing, are transferable across careers.
Students can make better choices by researching different majors, talking with seniors and professionals, and taking introductory courses. It is also comforting to remember that a major does not determine one's entire future. Many successful people work in fields completely unrelated to what they studied.

Video games are a popular form of entertainment among young people, but they have long been controversial. Parents and teachers worry that games waste time, encourage violence and lead to addiction.
There is some basis for these concerns. Excessive gaming can interfere with sleep, study and physical activity, and a small number of players develop serious problems controlling their gaming habits.
However, research also reveals benefits. Many games require players to solve complex problems, make quick decisions and cooperate with teammates. Some studies have found that certain action games improve attention and visual skills.
Games are increasingly used in education as well. Educational games make learning subjects such as history, mathematics and languages more interactive and enjoyable.
As with many things, the key is moderation. Playing games for a limited time, choosing suitable content and balancing gaming with other activities can allow young people to enjoy the benefits while avoiding the risks. Instead of banning games entirely, parents can talk with their children and set reasonable rules together.

Fast food is cheap, convenient and tasty, which explains its popularity among students and busy workers. However, regularly eating fast food can harm our health.
Most fast food is high in calories, fat, salt and sugar while being low in fibre, vitamins and minerals. A single meal of burger, fries and a soft drink can contain more than half the calories an adult needs for an entire day.
Over time, a diet based on fast food increases the risk of obesity, heart disease and diabetes. These conditions, once associated mainly with older people, are now appearing in younger populations.
It is not necessary to avoid fast food completely. The problem lies in frequency and choice. Many restaurants now offer healthier options, such as salads, grilled chicken and fruit. Choosing water instead of soft drinks also makes a big difference.
Cooking simple meals at home is another solution. It is usually cheaper and allows us to control the ingredients. With a little planning, eating well does not have to be difficult or time-consuming.

Honesty is one of the most widely respected values in every culture. Yet in daily life, people sometimes tell small lies to avoid trouble, gain advantages or protect others' feelings.
In the short term, dishonesty may seem convenient. A student might copy homework to save time, or a business might exaggerate the quality of its products to increase sales. But such behaviour carries long-term costs.
Trust, once lost, is very difficult to rebuild. A person known for lying will find it hard to maintain friendships or professional relationships. Companies caught cheating customers can lose their reputation overnight.
At the level of society, honesty reduces costs for everyone. When people can trust each other, they need fewer rules, checks and contracts, and cooperation becomes easier.
Being honest is not always easy, especially when the truth is unpleasant. However, it can be expressed with kindness and tact. In the end, honesty brings peace of mind, because honest people never have to remember what they said.

Nobody enjoys failing. A poor exam result or a rejected application can make us feel disappointed and embarrassed. Yet failure is an unavoidable part of life, and how we respond to it often determines our future success.
Psychologist Carol Dweck distinguishes between two mindsets. People with a "fixed mindset" believe that abilities are fixed, so failure seems to prove that they are not good enough. People with a "growth mindset" believe that abilities can be developed through effort, so they view failure as an opportunity to learn.
Research shows that students with a growth mindset are more likely to take on challenges and persist when tasks become difficult.
To learn from failure, it helps to analyse what went wrong without blaming yourself excessively. Was the problem a lack of preparation, a poor strategy or simply bad luck? What could be done differently next time?
History is full of people who failed many times before succeeding. Their stories remind us that failure is not the opposite of success, but often a necessary step toward it.

Earthquakes are among the most destructive natural disasters. In a matter of seconds, they can destroy buildings, roads and bridges, causing great loss of life.
The earth's outer layer is divided into large pieces called plates, which move slowly over time. When plates push against each other, pressure builds up. When the pressure is suddenly released, the ground shakes, producing an earthquake.
Scientists cannot yet predict exactly when and where an earthquake will occur. However, they can identify high-risk regions and estimate the likelihood of future earthquakes.
Preparation is therefore essential. Buildings in earthquake zones should be designed to withstand shaking. Early warning systems can detect the first waves and send alerts a few seconds before strong shaking arrives, giving people time to take cover.
Individuals should also know how to respond. During an earthquake, experts recommend "Drop, Cover and Hold On": get down, take cover under a sturdy table and hold on until the shaking stops. Knowing these simple steps can save lives.

Research suggests that people form an impression of others within the first few seconds of meeting them. Whether in a job interview or a social situation, first impressions can have a lasting effect.
Appearance plays a role. Dressing neatly and appropriately for the occasion shows respect and seriousness. This does not mean wearing expensive clothes, but rather looking clean and well-prepared.
Body language is equally important. A firm handshake, steady eye contact and a genuine smile communicate confidence and friendliness. Crossing your arms or looking at your phone can make you seem unfriendly or uninterested.
Punctuality also matters. Arriving late suggests carelessness, while arriving a few minutes early demonstrates reliability.
In conversation, listen actively and show interest in the other person. Asking thoughtful questions and remembering names make people feel valued.
While first impressions are powerful, they are not everything. Over time, people judge us by our actions and character. A good first impression opens the door, but sincerity and competence keep it open.

Ancient buildings, traditional crafts, folk music and local customs are all part of cultural heritage. They connect us with our ancestors and give communities a sense of identity.
Unfortunately, much heritage is under threat. Rapid urban development has led to the destruction of old neighbourhoods, while young people often leave villages where traditional skills are practised. Some crafts are in danger of disappearing because no one is willing to learn them.
Tourism can be both a blessing and a curse. It brings money for preservation and raises public awareness, but large crowds can damage fragile sites and turn living traditions into commercial performances.
Many countries have established laws and programmes to protect heritage. UNESCO lists important sites and practices to draw international attention and support.
Technology also offers new tools. Digital scanning can create detailed records of ancient buildings, and online platforms allow craftspeople to sell their products to a wider market.
Protecting heritage is a shared responsibility. By learning about our history and supporting traditional culture, we ensure that future generations can enjoy it too.

Homes consume a large share of the world's energy, mainly for heating, cooling, lighting and appliances. By making small changes, households can save money and reduce their impact on the environment.
Lighting is an easy place to start. LED bulbs use far less electricity than traditional bulbs and last many times longer. Turning off lights when leaving a room is a simple but effective habit.
Many electronic devices continue to use power even when switched off but still plugged in. Unplugging chargers and using power strips that can be switched off reduces this "standby" consumption.
Heating and air conditioning account for a large portion of energy use. Setting the air conditioner a degree or two higher in summer and closing curtains to block the sun can lead to significant savings.
When buying new appliances, choosing products with high energy-efficiency ratings pays off over time.
Individually, these steps may seem minor. But multiplied across millions of homes, they can reduce the need for power plants and help protect the planet.

Imagine being able to print a toy, a tool or even a house. This is no longer science fiction. Three-dimensional printing builds objects layer by layer from digital designs, using materials such as plastic, metal and concrete.
Unlike traditional manufacturing, which often requires expensive moulds and large factories, 3D printing makes it possible to produce small quantities of customized products at a reasonable cost.
The technology is already used in many fields. Doctors print models of organs to plan complex operations, and some patients receive custom-made artificial limbs and dental implants. Engineers print parts for aircraft that are lighter and stronger than conventional ones.
3D printing also reduces waste, because material is added only where it is needed rather than being cut away.
Nevertheless, challenges remain. Printing large objects is still slow, and the quality of some materials needs improvement. There are also concerns about people printing dangerous items.
As the technology matures, it may change not only how products are made but also where, bringing production closer to consumers.

t: Why Quitting Smoking Is Worth It
b:
Smoking is one of the leading causes of preventable death worldwide. It damages almost every organ of the body and greatly increases the risk of lung cancer, heart disease and stroke.
Smoking also harms people who do not smoke. Second-hand smoke is especially dangerous for children, who may develop breathing problems and infections.
Many smokers want to quit but find it extremely difficult because nicotine is highly addictive. However, the benefits of quitting begin almost immediately. Within days, the sense of taste and smell improves. Within months, breathing becomes easier, and over years the risk of serious disease falls substantially.
There are many ways to make quitting easier. Setting a specific quit date, avoiding situations that trigger the desire to smoke, and seeking support from friends or professional programmes all increase the chances of success.
Public policies such as banning smoking in public places and raising tobacco taxes have also helped reduce smoking rates.
It is never too late to quit. Every cigarette not smoked is a gift to one's health.

tc: 虚假新闻与批判性思维
b:
In the age of social media, information spreads faster than ever. Unfortunately, so does false information. Fake news stories, misleading headlines and edited photos can reach millions of people within hours.
Fake news is often designed to attract attention by provoking strong emotions such as anger or fear. People tend to share such stories quickly without checking whether they are true.
The consequences can be serious. False health advice may endanger lives, and rumours can damage reputations or cause public panic.
Developing critical thinking skills is the best defence. Before believing or sharing a story, ask a few questions: Who published it? Is the source reliable? Do other trustworthy media report the same thing? Is there evidence, or only opinion?
Be especially careful with headlines that seem too shocking to be true, as they often are.
Media platforms and governments also have responsibilities to limit the spread of misinformation. But ultimately, each of us is a gatekeeper. Thinking carefully before clicking "share" helps create a healthier information environment.

With so much information available online, some people wonder whether university libraries are still necessary. In fact, libraries are changing rather than disappearing.
Modern libraries provide much more than books. They offer access to academic databases, journals and e-books that are too expensive for individual students to buy. Librarians help students find reliable sources and avoid low-quality information online.
Libraries also serve as important study spaces. Many students find it easier to concentrate in a quiet library than in a noisy dormitory. Group study rooms allow teams to work on projects together.
Some libraries have added new facilities, such as computer labs, 3D printers and spaces for workshops and exhibitions, turning them into centres of learning and creativity.
During exam periods, finding a seat in the library can be a challenge, which shows how much students still value them.
Rather than being replaced by the Internet, libraries have become guides to it. They remain at the heart of academic life, supporting learning, research and the exchange of ideas.

Every living thing, from bacteria to humans, carries a set of instructions written in DNA. This long molecule, shaped like a twisted ladder, contains the information needed to build and maintain an organism.
The structure of DNA was discovered in 1953, a breakthrough that transformed biology. Since then, scientists have learned to read, copy and even edit genetic code.
Understanding DNA has brought many practical benefits. Doctors can identify genetic diseases early, and police can use DNA evidence to solve crimes. In agriculture, scientists have developed crops that resist disease and drought.
The completion of the Human Genome Project in 2003 provided a map of all human genes, opening the door to personalized medicine, in which treatments are designed according to a patient's genetic profile.
At the same time, genetic technology raises ethical questions. Should parents be allowed to choose their children's characteristics? Who should have access to a person's genetic information?
As our ability to read and change DNA grows, society must carefully consider how this powerful knowledge should be used.

Almost every job today involves working with others. From scientific research to film production, complex tasks require people with different skills to cooperate.
Effective teams achieve more than individuals working alone. Members can share ideas, check each other's work and divide tasks according to strengths. Diverse perspectives often lead to more creative solutions.
However, teamwork is not always smooth. Conflicts may arise from different opinions or working styles. Some members may contribute less than others, causing frustration.
Successful teams share several characteristics. They have clear goals, so everyone knows what they are working toward. Roles and responsibilities are defined, and communication is open and respectful. Members trust each other and feel safe expressing different opinions.
Good leadership also helps. A leader who listens, encourages participation and resolves conflicts fairly can bring out the best in a team.
For students, group projects provide valuable practice. Instead of seeing them as a burden, students can treat them as an opportunity to develop the cooperation skills that employers highly value.

Music has a remarkable ability to influence our emotions. A cheerful song can lift our mood, while a slow melody may bring tears to our eyes. But why does music affect us so deeply?
Scientists have found that listening to music activates many areas of the brain, including those related to emotion, memory and movement. Pleasant music triggers the release of dopamine, a chemical associated with pleasure and reward.
Music is also closely linked to memory. A song from our teenage years can instantly bring back vivid memories of people and places. This connection is so strong that music therapy is used to help patients with memory loss.
Across cultures, music serves social purposes. People sing together at celebrations, ceremonies and sports events, creating a sense of unity.
Many people use music to manage their daily lives: upbeat songs during exercise, calm music for studying or relaxing.
Whether we play an instrument or simply listen, music enriches our lives and connects us with others. It is truly a universal language.

Although water covers most of the earth, only a tiny fraction is fresh water available for human use. In many parts of the world, water shortages are becoming increasingly serious.
Population growth, expanding agriculture and industry, and climate change are all increasing pressure on water supplies. Some major rivers no longer reach the sea during dry seasons, and underground water levels are falling in many regions.
Pollution makes the problem worse. Waste from factories and farms contaminates rivers and lakes, making water unsafe to drink.
Agriculture uses the largest share of fresh water, so improving irrigation is crucial. Methods such as drip irrigation deliver water directly to plant roots and greatly reduce waste.
Cities can repair leaking pipes and recycle wastewater for uses such as watering parks.
At home, everyone can save water by taking shorter showers, turning off the tap while brushing teeth and fixing leaks promptly. Water is the source of life. Using it wisely today ensures that future generations will have enough tomorrow.

In many Chinese cities, it is now possible to go for days without touching cash. People pay for meals, taxis and even street food simply by scanning a code with their phones.
Mobile payment offers obvious convenience. There is no need to carry a wallet or wait for change, and transactions are recorded automatically, making it easier to track spending.
For businesses, digital payment reduces the risk of theft and saves time counting money. It has also helped small vendors reach more customers.
However, a cashless society also raises concerns. Elderly people who are not familiar with smartphones may find it difficult to pay for basic services. Technical failures or a lost phone can leave people unable to buy anything.
Privacy is another issue, because every digital transaction leaves a record that can be collected and analysed.
For these reasons, many experts argue that cash should remain available as an option. A truly modern payment system should be convenient for the majority while still including everyone.

When people think about improving their health, they often imagine dramatic changes such as strict diets or intensive training. Yet research suggests that small, consistent habits may be more effective in the long run.
Simple actions like taking the stairs instead of the lift, walking for ten minutes after meals or adding a portion of vegetables to dinner may seem trivial. But repeated every day, they add up to significant benefits.
Small habits are easier to maintain because they require little willpower. Dramatic changes often fail because they are too difficult to sustain, leading people to give up entirely.
One useful strategy is "habit stacking": attaching a new habit to an existing one. For example, you could do a few stretches after brushing your teeth or drink a glass of water before each meal.
Tracking progress can also increase motivation. Seeing a calendar filled with successful days encourages people to keep going.
Health is not built in a day. It is the result of countless small choices, and every good choice counts.

More and more families keep pets such as dogs and cats. For many owners, pets are not merely animals but beloved members of the family.
Research suggests that pets can benefit human health. Stroking a pet can lower blood pressure and reduce stress. Dog owners tend to exercise more because they walk their dogs every day.
Pets also provide companionship, which is especially valuable for elderly people living alone. Caring for an animal gives a sense of purpose and routine. For children, looking after a pet teaches responsibility and empathy.
However, owning a pet also involves serious commitments. Pets need food, medical care, training and attention for many years. Unfortunately, some animals are abandoned when owners lose interest or face difficulties.
Responsible ownership is therefore essential. Before getting a pet, people should consider whether they have enough time, space and money. Adopting animals from shelters is also a kind choice.
When treated with care, the bond between humans and animals brings joy to both.

Many universities have debate clubs where students argue for or against a motion, such as whether homework should be banned. Debating is more than a competition; it is an excellent way to develop thinking skills.
To prepare for a debate, students must research a topic thoroughly, gather evidence and anticipate the arguments of the other side. This process teaches them to evaluate information critically and to distinguish facts from opinions.
Debaters often have to argue for positions they personally disagree with. While this may seem strange, it helps them understand different perspectives and avoid narrow thinking.
Debating also improves communication. Speakers learn to organize ideas logically, express them clearly under time pressure and respond quickly to unexpected questions.
In addition, debate teaches respect. A good debater attacks arguments, not people, and listens carefully to opponents.
These skills are valuable far beyond the debate room. Whether in a job interview, a business meeting or a discussion with friends, the ability to think clearly and argue persuasively is a great advantage.

It is a question that almost every child asks: why is the sky blue? The answer lies in the way sunlight interacts with the air.
Sunlight looks white, but it is actually made up of all the colours of the rainbow. Each colour has a different wavelength; red light has a longer wavelength, while blue light has a shorter one.
When sunlight enters the atmosphere, it collides with tiny gas molecules. These molecules scatter shorter wavelengths much more strongly than longer ones. As a result, blue light is scattered in all directions across the sky, and that is the colour we see when we look up.
At sunrise and sunset, the sun is low, and its light must travel through much more air to reach our eyes. Most of the blue light is scattered away before it arrives, leaving the reds and oranges that make sunsets so beautiful.
Simple questions often lead to fascinating science. Staying curious about everyday phenomena is the first step to understanding the world.

Working from home, once rare, has become common in many industries. Many employees appreciate the flexibility and the time saved by not commuting.
Remote work offers clear advantages. Workers can organize their schedules more freely, and some find that they concentrate better without office distractions. Companies can save on office space and hire talented people regardless of location.
However, working from home also brings challenges. The boundary between work and personal life can become blurred, leading some people to work longer hours. Others feel isolated without daily contact with colleagues.
Communication may also suffer. Quick conversations that happen naturally in an office require scheduled video calls, and misunderstandings occur more easily.
To work effectively from home, experts suggest creating a dedicated workspace, keeping regular hours and taking breaks. Staying in contact with colleagues through regular check-ins helps maintain team spirit.
Many organizations now adopt a hybrid model, combining days in the office with days at home. This approach aims to offer the best of both worlds.

Chinese calligraphy is much more than beautiful handwriting. It is considered one of the highest forms of art in Chinese culture, combining visual beauty with personal expression.
Using a brush, ink and paper, calligraphers create characters with strokes of varying thickness and rhythm. Each style, from the formal regular script to the flowing cursive script, conveys a different mood.
Learning calligraphy requires patience and discipline. Beginners spend years copying the works of great masters, practising basic strokes again and again. Through this process, they develop not only skill but also concentration and calmness.
Traditionally, it was believed that a person's handwriting reflected their character. A calligrapher's work reveals their personality, emotions and state of mind at the moment of writing.
In the digital age, when most people type rather than write, calligraphy has become less common in daily life. Yet interest remains strong, and many schools offer calligraphy classes.
Practising calligraphy offers a quiet escape from the fast pace of modern life and a deeper connection with Chinese culture.
