Roughly one third of all food produced in the world is lost or wasted. At the same time, hundreds of millions of people do not have enough to eat.
Food is wasted at every stage. On farms, crops may be left unharvested if they do not meet appearance standards. In shops, products are thrown away when they approach their expiration dates. At home and in restaurants, people buy and cook more than they can eat.
Wasting food also wastes the water, land and energy used to produce it. Furthermore, food rotting in landfills releases methane, a powerful greenhouse gas.
Many people have joined campaigns to finish their meals and avoid ordering too much. Restaurants offer smaller portions, and some supermarkets sell imperfect fruit and vegetables at lower prices.
At home, planning meals, making shopping lists and storing food properly can greatly reduce waste. Leftovers can be creatively turned into new dishes.
Valuing food means respecting the efforts of farmers and the resources of our planet.

At the start of each term, many students make ambitious plans: read twenty books, exercise every day, improve their English dramatically. A few weeks later, most of these goals have been forgotten.
One reason is that the goals are too vague. "Improve my English" gives no clear direction. A better goal is specific and measurable, such as "learn fifteen new words a day and review them every evening".
Goals should also be realistic. Setting targets that are too high leads to disappointment and loss of motivation. It is better to start small and gradually increase the challenge.
Breaking a large goal into steps with deadlines makes progress visible. Preparing for CET-4, for example, could be divided into vocabulary, listening, reading and writing practice, each with a weekly plan.
Writing goals down and sharing them with a friend increases commitment. Regularly reviewing progress allows you to adjust plans when necessary.
Finally, celebrate small achievements along the way. Recognizing progress keeps motivation high and turns a long journey into a series of manageable and rewarding steps.

Driverless cars, once a dream of science fiction, are now being tested on roads in many cities. Using cameras, radar and artificial intelligence, these vehicles can detect their surroundings and make driving decisions without human input.
Supporters believe self-driving cars could dramatically reduce accidents, since most crashes are caused by human error such as distraction, fatigue or drunk driving. They could also give elderly and disabled people greater independence.
Driverless technology might ease traffic jams as well. Vehicles that communicate with each other can travel closer together and choose more efficient routes.
However, many challenges remain. Driverless cars must handle unexpected situations, such as road construction, bad weather or unpredictable pedestrians. Questions of responsibility are also complicated: if a self-driving car causes an accident, who is to blame?
Public trust is another issue. Many people still feel uncomfortable letting a machine take full control.
It may take years before driverless cars become common, but they are likely to transform transport and the shape of our cities.

Many students today spend hours every day looking at screens, whether for study or entertainment. As a result, eye strain and short-sightedness have become increasingly common, especially among young people.
Symptoms of eye strain include dry eyes, blurred vision and headaches. Looking at screens for long periods causes us to blink less often, which leads to dryness.
Eye doctors recommend the "20-20-20" rule: every twenty minutes, look at something twenty feet away for twenty seconds. This simple habit allows the eye muscles to relax.
Spending time outdoors is also important. Research has found that children who spend more time in natural daylight are less likely to develop short-sightedness.
Proper lighting matters too. Avoid reading in dim light or using a bright screen in a dark room. Keep screens at a comfortable distance, about an arm's length away.
Regular eye examinations can detect problems early. Our eyes work hard for us every waking moment, and a little care can help keep them healthy for life.

t: Following the Rules of the Road
b:
Traffic accidents kill more than a million people around the world every year, and many more are seriously injured. Most of these accidents could be prevented if people followed basic traffic rules.
Common dangerous behaviours include speeding, running red lights and using mobile phones while driving or walking. Looking at a phone for just a few seconds while driving means travelling a considerable distance without watching the road.
Pedestrians and cyclists also have responsibilities. Crossing the road at zebra crossings, waiting for the green light and wearing helmets when riding electric bikes can save lives.
Some people break the rules because they are in a hurry or think nothing will happen to them. But saving a minute is never worth risking a life.
Governments use cameras, fines and education campaigns to improve road safety. Good road design, such as clear signs and separate lanes for bicycles, also helps.
Ultimately, safety depends on everyone. Respecting traffic rules is a sign of responsibility, protecting not only ourselves but also others.

When we hear the word "bacteria", we often think of disease. However, the vast majority of bacteria are harmless, and many are essential to life.
The human body is home to trillions of bacteria, most of them living in the gut. These tiny organisms help digest food, produce certain vitamins and protect us from harmful germs. Scientists have discovered that the balance of gut bacteria may even influence our mood and immune system.
Bacteria also play a crucial role in nature. They break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the soil. Without them, the earth would be covered with waste.
Humans have used bacteria for thousands of years to make foods such as yoghurt, cheese and pickles. Today, bacteria are used to produce medicines and clean up oil spills.
Excessive use of antibacterial products and antibiotics can disturb the natural balance, killing helpful bacteria along with harmful ones.
Instead of trying to eliminate all bacteria, we should learn to live in harmony with these invisible partners.

In an increasingly connected world, we interact with people from different cultures more often than ever. Understanding cultural differences can prevent misunderstandings and build better relationships.
Cultures differ in many ways. In some countries, people express opinions directly, while in others, indirect communication is considered more polite. Attitudes toward time vary as well: in certain cultures punctuality is extremely important, while in others schedules are more flexible.
Even gestures can have different meanings. A gesture that is friendly in one place may be rude in another.
Misunderstandings often arise when we judge others by the standards of our own culture. Something that seems strange or impolite may be completely normal elsewhere.
The best approach is to remain curious and open-minded. Observing how local people behave, asking questions respectfully and learning a few words of their language show goodwill.
Cultural differences are not obstacles but opportunities. By learning from each other, we enrich our own perspectives and discover that, beneath the surface, people everywhere share similar hopes and values.

As cities expand, natural habitats disappear, and many animals lose their homes. In recent years, however, urban planners have started to think about how to make cities friendlier to nature.
Green roofs covered with plants are one solution. They provide habitats for birds and insects, absorb rainwater and keep buildings cooler in summer.
Parks and green corridors that connect different natural areas allow animals to move safely through the city. Some cities have restored rivers that were once hidden under concrete, bringing back fish and birds.
Residents can contribute too. Planting native flowers on balconies, putting up bird boxes and avoiding chemical pesticides in gardens help create small refuges for wildlife.
These efforts benefit people as well. Contact with nature reduces stress and improves well-being, and children who grow up near green spaces develop a stronger connection with the natural world.
A city does not have to be a concrete desert. With thoughtful design, it can become a place where people and nature live side by side.

Email remains one of the most important tools for communication at work and in university. A well-written email can make a positive impression, while a careless one may cause confusion or even offence.
A professional email starts with a clear subject line that summarizes its purpose, such as "Request for Meeting on Friday". This helps the recipient understand its importance at a glance.
The greeting should be appropriate. When writing to a professor or a manager, use their title and surname rather than a casual "Hi".
The body should be concise and well-organized. State your purpose in the first sentence or two, provide necessary details and make any request clear. Long paragraphs are difficult to read, so keep them short.
Pay attention to tone. Polite expressions like "Could you please" and "I would appreciate it if" sound respectful.
Before sending, always check spelling, grammar and attachments. Finally, end with a polite closing and your full name.
Taking an extra minute to write carefully shows respect for the reader and reflects well on you.

When you store photos online, stream a film or edit a document with classmates in real time, you are using cloud computing. But what exactly is "the cloud"?
In simple terms, cloud computing means using computing resources, such as storage and processing power, that are located in large data centres rather than on your own device. You access these resources through the Internet.
The cloud offers many advantages. Users can access their files from any device, anywhere. Businesses no longer need to buy and maintain expensive servers; instead, they pay for what they use, much like paying for electricity.
Cloud services also make collaboration easier, since multiple people can work on the same file simultaneously.
However, relying on the cloud has risks. Without an Internet connection, access may be limited. Data stored on remote servers may also be vulnerable to hacking or service failures.
To use the cloud safely, users should choose reliable providers, protect accounts with strong passwords and keep backups of important files. The cloud is invisible, but its influence on our lives is enormous.

t: The Benefits of Spending Time Outdoors
b:
Modern people spend most of their time indoors, moving from home to classroom or office and back again. Yet spending time outdoors offers important benefits for both body and mind.
Sunlight helps the body produce vitamin D, which is essential for strong bones and a healthy immune system. Natural light also regulates our internal clock, helping us sleep better at night.
Being in nature reduces stress. Studies show that a walk in a park can lower levels of stress hormones and improve mood more than a walk along a busy street. Some doctors have even begun "prescribing" time in nature.
Outdoor activities often involve physical movement, whether hiking, cycling or simply playing. They also provide opportunities to socialize with friends and family.
For students who spend long hours studying, short outdoor breaks can restore attention and creativity.
You do not need to travel to a national park to enjoy these benefits. A nearby park, a tree-lined street or a campus garden will do. Make it a habit to step outside every day.

Respecting the elderly is a traditional virtue in Chinese culture. Older people have contributed to society for decades and possess valuable knowledge and experience.
In modern society, however, the elderly sometimes feel left behind. Rapid technological change makes it difficult for some to use smartphones, online services and self-service machines. Many live alone because their children work in other cities.
Respect can be shown in many practical ways. Young people can help older relatives learn to use technology patiently. Visiting or calling regularly reduces loneliness. In public, offering a seat on the bus or helping someone cross the road is a simple act of kindness.
Society also has a role to play. Designing services that are easy for older people to use, keeping alternatives to digital systems and creating community activities can help them remain active and included.
Respecting the elderly is not only about the past but also about the future. One day, we will all grow old, and the way we treat older people today reflects the kind of society we hope to live in.

Listening is often the most challenging part of English exams for Chinese students. Unlike reading, you cannot go back and check a word you missed. However, with the right methods, listening skills can improve steadily.
First, listen regularly. Short daily practice is more effective than occasional long sessions. Even fifteen minutes a day of news, podcasts or recorded lectures will make a difference over time.
Second, combine intensive and extensive listening. Intensive listening means studying a short passage carefully, repeating it until you understand every word, perhaps by writing down what you hear. Extensive listening means enjoying longer materials for general understanding without worrying about every detail.
Third, learn how words sound in connected speech. Native speakers often link words together and weaken unstressed sounds, so familiar words may become hard to recognize.
Fourth, build vocabulary, because you cannot understand words you do not know.
Finally, during the exam, read the questions before listening and predict what you might hear. Patience and persistence are the keys to success.

Have you noticed that time seems to pass more quickly as you grow older? A summer holiday felt endless when you were a child, but now months disappear in a flash.
Psychologists have several explanations. One theory suggests that our sense of time depends on how many new memories we form. Children experience many things for the first time, creating rich memories that make a period feel long. Adults follow familiar routines, forming fewer distinct memories, so time seems to shrink when we look back.
Another explanation is proportional: one year is a fifth of a five-year-old's life but only a fiftieth of a fifty-year-old's life.
Emotions also affect our perception. Time drags when we are bored or anxious, but flies when we are absorbed in something enjoyable.
If you want time to feel richer, try to fill it with new experiences: visit unfamiliar places, learn a new skill or meet new people. Novelty not only makes life more interesting but also seems to stretch our sense of time.

In a competitive society, many people work long hours, answer emails late at night and rarely take holidays. While hard work is admirable, neglecting other parts of life can have serious consequences.
Overwork is linked to exhaustion, stress-related illness and damaged relationships. Ironically, it can also reduce productivity, because tired people make more mistakes and have fewer creative ideas.
Achieving balance begins with setting boundaries. This might mean not checking work messages after a certain time or keeping weekends for family and hobbies.
Learning to say no is also important. Accepting every request leads to an impossible workload. Prioritizing tasks and delegating when possible can free up time.
Companies play a role as well. Flexible schedules, reasonable workloads and a culture that respects personal time help employees stay healthy and motivated.
Work-life balance does not mean dividing time equally. It means making sure that work does not crowd out health, relationships and personal growth. A balanced life is not only happier but often more successful.

Museums are treasure houses of human history, art and science. In recent years, visiting museums has become increasingly popular among young people in China.
A museum visit allows us to see objects that we have only read about in textbooks: ancient bronze vessels, delicate porcelain, dinosaur fossils and paintings by great masters. Seeing the real thing creates a deeper impression than any picture.
Modern museums have also become more interactive. Touch screens, virtual reality and creative activities make history come alive. Some museums have become famous on social media for their creative products, such as cultural souvenirs inspired by ancient artworks.
To get the most out of a visit, it helps to plan ahead. Choose a few galleries to focus on rather than trying to see everything. Audio guides and guided tours provide valuable background information.
Museums are not only for experts. They welcome anyone with curiosity. Spending an afternoon among the treasures of the past can be both educational and relaxing, reminding us of where we come from.

Heatwaves, heavy storms, floods and droughts are becoming more frequent and intense in many parts of the world. Scientists link this trend to climate change.
Extreme weather can disrupt transport, damage homes and threaten lives. Preparing in advance can greatly reduce the harm.
Individuals should pay attention to weather warnings and take them seriously. During a heatwave, stay indoors during the hottest hours, drink plenty of water and check on elderly neighbours. During heavy rain, avoid low-lying areas and never drive through flooded roads.
It is wise to prepare an emergency kit with water, food, a torch, batteries, medicine and important documents.
Cities are also adapting. Some are improving drainage systems, creating "sponge" areas that absorb rainwater, and planting trees to reduce heat.
While we work to limit climate change, we must also learn to live with its effects. Preparation, awareness and community cooperation can make us more resilient in the face of nature's power.

Taking selfies has become a global phenomenon. People photograph themselves at tourist sites, restaurants and gatherings, then share the images on social media.
Selfies can be a positive form of self-expression and a way to record memories and share experiences with friends.
However, the selfie culture also has a darker side. Many people edit their photos heavily to appear thinner or more attractive, creating unrealistic standards of beauty. Constantly comparing oneself to these idealized images can damage self-esteem, particularly among young people.
The desire for the perfect selfie has even led to dangerous behaviour, with people taking risks near cliffs, traffic or wild animals.
Moreover, some argue that focusing on taking pictures prevents people from fully enjoying the moment. Instead of watching a beautiful sunset, they watch their screens.
There is nothing wrong with taking selfies in moderation. The key is to remember that our value does not depend on the number of likes we receive, and that some moments are best experienced rather than recorded.

Back and neck pain used to be problems mainly for older people, but they are increasingly common among students and office workers. The main cause is poor posture during long hours of sitting.
When we bend our heads to look at phones, the neck must support a much heavier load than when the head is upright. Over time, this places strain on the muscles and spine.
Improving posture begins with your workspace. Your screen should be at eye level, your feet flat on the floor and your back supported by the chair. Keep your shoulders relaxed rather than raised.
Movement is just as important as posture. Experts advise standing up and stretching every thirty to forty-five minutes. Simple exercises, such as rolling the shoulders and gently turning the head, can relieve tension.
Strengthening the core muscles through activities like swimming or yoga provides better support for the spine.
If pain persists, it is wise to consult a doctor. Taking care of your back now will prevent more serious problems in the future.

In modern cities, many people do not know their neighbours. They pass each other in the lift every day without saying hello. Yet strong communities bring many benefits.
Neighbours who know each other can help in emergencies, look after each other's homes and support elderly residents. Communities with strong social ties tend to be safer and happier.
Building connections does not require much. Greeting neighbours, introducing yourself to newcomers and joining community activities are simple first steps.
Many communities now organize events such as festival celebrations, book exchanges and volunteer clean-ups. Online groups allow residents to share information, lend tools and organize group purchases.
Shared spaces also matter. Parks, playgrounds and community gardens give people places to meet and interact naturally.
In a fast-paced world, it is easy to feel isolated. But by making small efforts to connect with those around us, we can turn a group of buildings into a real community where people care for one another.

Writing is an important part of the CET-4 exam, and many students find it challenging. However, a few practical strategies can significantly improve your essays.
First, read the question carefully and make sure you understand what is required. Many students lose marks simply because they write off topic.
Second, spend a few minutes planning before you write. A clear structure, with an introduction, two or three body paragraphs and a conclusion, makes your essay easier to follow.
Third, each body paragraph should begin with a topic sentence stating its main idea, followed by explanations and examples. Specific examples make arguments more convincing.
Fourth, use linking words such as "however", "moreover" and "as a result" to connect ideas smoothly.
Fifth, aim for accuracy rather than complexity. Simple sentences with correct grammar are better than complicated ones full of errors. Use a variety of vocabulary, but only words you are confident about.
Finally, leave time to check your work for spelling and grammar mistakes. Regular practice, along with reading good model essays, will steadily improve your writing.

For centuries, people have looked at the stars and wondered whether we are alone in the universe. Today, scientists are seriously searching for an answer.
The universe is unimaginably large, containing billions of galaxies, each with billions of stars. Astronomers have discovered thousands of planets orbiting other stars, some located in "habitable zones" where liquid water could exist.
Within our own solar system, several places are considered possible homes for simple life. Mars once had rivers and lakes, and some moons of Jupiter and Saturn appear to have oceans beneath their icy surfaces.
Scientists search for signs of life in various ways: sending rovers to collect samples, analysing the atmospheres of distant planets and listening for radio signals.
So far, no evidence of life beyond Earth has been confirmed. But many scientists believe that, given the vast number of planets, life may well exist elsewhere.
Discovering even a simple microbe on another world would be one of the greatest discoveries in human history, changing how we see our place in the universe.

Giving gifts is a common way to express affection, gratitude and respect. However, customs surrounding gifts vary greatly from culture to culture.
In China, gifts are often presented with both hands as a sign of respect, and the receiver may politely decline several times before accepting. Some items are traditionally avoided; for example, giving a clock may be considered unlucky.
In many Western countries, people usually open gifts immediately in front of the giver and express their thanks enthusiastically. In some cultures, the wrapping and presentation of a gift are as important as the gift itself.
Despite these differences, the meaning of a gift lies mainly in the thought behind it. An expensive gift chosen carelessly may mean less than a simple handmade card that shows real understanding of the receiver.
Thoughtful gifts reflect the interests and needs of the person receiving them. Sometimes the best gift is not an object at all, but time and attention: a shared meal, a helping hand or a heartfelt letter.

Forests cover about a third of the earth's land and are home to most of the world's land animals and plants. They are often called "the lungs of the earth".
Forests provide countless benefits. They absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen, helping to regulate the climate. Their roots hold soil in place, preventing erosion and landslides, and they protect water sources by regulating the flow of rivers.
Forests also support human livelihoods, providing wood, food and medicine. Hundreds of millions of people depend directly on forests for their living.
However, large areas of forest are still being cut down for farming, logging and development. Losing forests releases stored carbon and destroys habitats, pushing many species toward extinction.
Encouragingly, reforestation efforts are making progress. China, for instance, has carried out large-scale tree-planting programmes that have significantly increased forest coverage over recent decades.
Protecting existing forests and restoring damaged ones are among the most effective ways to fight climate change and preserve biodiversity.

In the past, people often learned a trade when they were young and practised it for the rest of their lives. Today, technology and the economy change so rapidly that the knowledge we gain at university may become outdated within a few years.
This is why lifelong learning has become essential. It means continuing to acquire new knowledge and skills throughout life, whether for career development or personal fulfilment.
Fortunately, learning opportunities are more accessible than ever. Online courses, podcasts, e-books and video tutorials allow people to learn almost anything at their own pace, often for free.
Lifelong learning brings benefits beyond employment. Learning new things keeps the mind active, may protect against memory decline in old age and brings a sense of achievement.
The most important requirement is a curious and open attitude. Lifelong learners are not afraid to admit what they do not know and are willing to step outside their comfort zones.
As the saying goes, "Live and learn." In a changing world, the ability to keep learning may be the most valuable skill of all.

Vocabulary is the foundation of language. Without enough words, even the best grammar cannot help you express ideas or understand others.
For CET-4 candidates, a solid vocabulary affects every part of the exam. In reading, unfamiliar words slow you down and lead to misunderstanding. In listening, you cannot catch words you do not recognize. In writing and translation, a limited vocabulary makes your expression repetitive.
Memorizing long word lists, however, is often boring and ineffective. Words learned in isolation are easily forgotten. A better approach is to learn words in context. When you meet a new word in an article, notice how it is used, which words commonly appear with it and what it means in that particular sentence.
Many words have several meanings. The word "address", for example, can refer to where someone lives, a formal speech or the act of dealing with a problem. Context tells you which meaning is intended.
Review is also essential. Revisiting words at increasing intervals helps move them into long-term memory. With daily reading and regular review, your vocabulary will grow steadily and naturally.

Kindness does not have to be grand to be meaningful. Holding a door for someone, thanking a delivery worker or helping a lost tourist find their way may take only a moment, yet it can brighten someone's day.
Research suggests that kindness benefits the giver as much as the receiver. Performing kind acts releases chemicals in the brain that make us feel happier and more connected to others. People who regularly help others report lower levels of stress.
Kindness is also contagious. When people witness or receive kindness, they are more likely to be kind to others, creating a positive chain reaction.
In busy modern life, it is easy to become focused on our own concerns and overlook the people around us. Making kindness a habit requires awareness: noticing when someone needs help and being willing to act.
Some people practise "random acts of kindness", such as paying for a stranger's coffee or leaving encouraging notes.
The world can sometimes seem harsh, but each of us has the power to make it a little warmer. As the saying goes, no act of kindness, however small, is ever wasted.
